subtopics.title: Project Cash Flow, Interest & Time Value of Money
subtopics.subtitle: Cash-flow diagrams, simple vs compound interest, effective rates and interest factors

concepts.text: Project Cash Flow and Cash-Flow Diagrams

A project cash flow is the stream of money receipts (inflows) and disbursements (outflows) that a project generates over its life. Typical outflows are the first cost of land, buildings and equipment, operating and maintenance (O&M) costs and taxes; typical inflows are revenues, cost savings and the salvage value at the end of life. Net cash flow for a period is inflows minus outflows. Engineering economics compares projects by converting these time-scattered amounts to a common basis using an interest rate.
Conventions for drawing a cash-flow diagram:
items: A horizontal time line divided into periods 0, 1, 2, ... n; time 0 is the present (start of period 1).
Upward arrows are inflows (receipts, benefits); downward arrows are outflows (costs), drawn from the viewpoint of one party.
End-of-period convention: cash flows occurring during a period are assumed to occur at its end.
P = present amount at time 0, F = future amount at time n, A = uniform amount at the end of each period 1 to n, G = arithmetic gradient.

concepts.text: Interest and the Time Value of Money

Money has time value because it can earn a return if invested now: Rs 1,000 today is worth more than Rs 1,000 a year later. Interest is the price paid for the use of borrowed money, and the interest rate expresses it as a percentage of the principal per period. The discount rate is the rate used to bring future amounts back to present value; for a firm it is normally its MARR or cost of capital.

concepts.plainText: F = P(1 + i)^n and P = F / (1 + i)^n

concepts.text: Nominal, Effective and Continuous Rates

A nominal rate r is the annual rate quoted without accounting for compounding within the year, e.g. 12% per year compounded monthly. The effective annual rate is the rate actually earned when the sub-period interest is compounded m times a year. Effective rate always exceeds nominal rate when m > 1, and the gap grows as compounding becomes more frequent, approaching the continuous-compounding limit. For example, 12% compounded monthly gives (1.01)^12 − 1 = 12.68%, quarterly gives 12.55%, and 10% compounded continuously gives e^0.10 − 1 = 10.52%.

concepts.plainText: i_eff = (1 + r/m)^m − 1; continuous compounding: i = e^r − 1

concepts.text: Equivalence and Interest Factors

Two cash flows are equivalent at a given interest rate if they have the same value when moved to the same point in time. Equivalence depends on the interest rate: amounts equivalent at 10% are not equivalent at 12%. Standard factors, written in functional notation such as (P/A, i, n), convert one type of cash flow to another and are tabulated in textbooks.

Worked examples at i = 10% per year
1) Rs 50,000 due in 5 years: P = 50,000 / 1.1^5 = Rs 31,046
2) Rs 1,000 per year for 5 years: P = 1,000 x 3.7908 = Rs 3,791
3) Loan Rs 5,00,000 repaid in 5 equal annual instalments:
   A = 5,00,000 x (A/P,10%,5) = 5,00,000 x 0.26380 = Rs 1,31,899
4) Sinking fund for Rs 1,00,000 in 5 years at 8%:
   A = 1,00,000 x 0.08 / (1.08^5 − 1) = Rs 17,046
5) Gradient: Rs 1,000 in year 1 rising Rs 200/yr for 4 years:
   P = 1,000(P/A,10%,4) + 200(P/G,10%,4)
     = 1,000 x 3.1699 + 200 x 4.3781 = Rs 4,045
Useful relationships between factors:
items: Each factor pair is reciprocal: F/P = 1/(P/F), P/A = 1/(A/P), F/A = 1/(A/F).
A/P = A/F + i, so capital recovery equals sinking fund plus interest.
P/A approaches 1/i as n becomes very large; this gives the capitalised-cost formula P = A/i.
For an arithmetic gradient the first gradient amount G occurs at the end of period 2, not period 1.

notes.text: In numerical MCQs first identify what is given (P, F or A) and what is asked, then pick the matching factor. Draw a quick cash-flow diagram to check that the present amount is at time 0 and uniform amounts start at the end of period 1.
Do not mix periods and rates: if interest compounds monthly, either use the monthly rate r/m with n in months, or convert to the effective annual rate and use n in years.
Simple interest ignores interest on interest; for multi-year project evaluation always use compound interest unless the question explicitly states simple interest.

formulas.title: Compound amount
formulas.description: Future value of a single present amount P after n periods at interest rate i per period.

formulas.title: Effective annual rate
formulas.description: Converts a nominal annual rate r compounded m times a year into the rate actually earned per year.

formulas.title: Uniform-series present worth
formulas.description: Present worth at time 0 of n equal end-of-period amounts A.

formulas.title: Capital recovery
formulas.description: Equal annual amount that recovers a present investment P with interest over n periods, e.g. a loan instalment.

formulas.title: Sinking fund
formulas.description: Equal end-of-period deposit needed to accumulate a future sum F in n periods.

flashcards.front: What does an upward arrow mean on a cash-flow diagram?
flashcards.back: A cash inflow (receipt or benefit) at that point in time; downward arrows are outflows such as first cost and O&M costs.

flashcards.front: Why is the effective interest rate higher than the nominal rate?
flashcards.back: Because interest earned in each sub-period is itself compounded within the year; effective rate = (1 + r/m)^m − 1, which exceeds r whenever m > 1.

flashcards.front: What is the relation between the capital recovery and sinking fund factors?
flashcards.back: A/P = A/F + i: capital recovery equals the sinking fund factor plus the interest rate.
Different cash flows at different times are equivalent if they have equal value at a common point in time for a given interest rate.

questions.questionText: Rs 10,000 is deposited at 10% per year compounded annually. What is the amount after 3 years?
questions.explanation: F = P(1 + i)^n = 10,000 × 1.1^3 = Rs 13,310. Rs 13,000 would be the simple-interest answer.

questions.questionText: A bank quotes a nominal interest rate of 12% per year compounded monthly. The effective annual interest rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: i_eff = (1 + 0.12/12)^12 − 1 = 1.01^12 − 1 = 0.1268, i.e. 12.68%. 12.55% corresponds to quarterly compounding.

questions.questionText: What is the present worth of Rs 1,000 received at the end of each year for 5 years if the interest rate is 10% per year?
An engineer borrows Rs 5,00,000 at 10% per year, to be repaid in 5 equal end-of-year instalments. The annual instalment is approximately:
Two cash-flow series are said to be economically equivalent when:
options: They have the same value at a common point in time at a specified interest rate
They occur over the same number of years
They have the same first cost
questions.explanation: Equivalence means equal worth when both are moved to the same time using the given interest rate; it changes if the interest rate changes.

subtopics.title: Discounted Payback, NPV, IRR & MARR
subtopics.subtitle: MARR, simple and discounted payback, NPV, IRR interpolation, B/C ratio, decision rules

concepts.text: Discount Rate and MARR

The minimum attractive rate of return (MARR), also called the hurdle rate, is the lowest rate of return an organisation will accept on a new investment. It is used as the discount rate when computing present worth. A project is economically worth doing only if it earns at least the MARR, because otherwise the money could be put to a better use elsewhere.
Factors on which the MARR is based:
items: Cost of capital: the weighted average cost of debt (loan interest) and equity (shareholders' expected return).
Opportunity cost: the return on the best alternative investment forgone.
Project risk: riskier projects are assigned a higher MARR (risk premium).
Inflation expectations, availability of funds and management policy.

concepts.text: Simple and Discounted Payback Period

The simple payback period is the time needed for cumulative undiscounted net cash inflows to recover the initial investment. It ignores the time value of money and all cash flows after the payback point. The discounted payback period first discounts each year's cash flow at the MARR and then finds when the cumulative present worth becomes zero; it is always longer than the simple payback for a conventional project. Both are measures of liquidity and risk rather than of profitability.

Investment Rs 10,000; inflow Rs 4,000/yr for 4 years; MARR 10%
Year  Cash flow  PW at 10%  Cumulative PW
 0    -10,000    -10,000     -10,000
 1     +4,000     +3,636      -6,364
 2     +4,000     +3,306      -3,058
 3     +4,000     +3,005        -53
 4     +4,000     +2,732      +2,679
Simple payback     = 10,000 / 4,000 = 2.5 years
Discounted payback = 3 + 53 / 2,732 ≈ 3.02 years
NPV at 10%         = +Rs 2,679
Net Present Value (Present Worth)

Net present value (NPV), or present worth (PW), is the sum of all cash flows discounted to time 0 at the MARR. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the MARR and adds that much value in today's money. NPV is additive across projects, uses all cash flows and accounts for time value, which makes it the most reliable single criterion. Its drawback is that it needs a chosen discount rate and does not show the rate of return directly.

concepts.plainText: NPV = sum over t = 0..n of CF_t / (1 + i)^t

concepts.text: Internal Rate of Return

The internal rate of return (IRR) is the interest rate at which the NPV of a project's cash flows equals zero, i.e. the present worth of inflows equals the present worth of outflows. It is found by trial: compute NPV at two rates, one giving a positive and one a negative NPV, then interpolate linearly between them. In the table example NPV is +355 at 20% and −25 at 22%, so IRR ≈ 20 + 2 × 355/380 = 21.87% (exact 21.86%). A non-conventional cash flow with several sign changes may have more than one IRR.
Benefit-Cost Ratio and Decision Rules

The benefit-cost (B/C) ratio is widely used for public-sector projects such as roads, irrigation and hydropower. It divides the present (or annual) worth of benefits to the public by the present (or annual) worth of costs to the sponsor. In the modified B/C ratio, O&M costs are subtracted from benefits in the numerator instead of being added to costs.

rows: Ignores time value and later cash flows

concepts.text: The NPV profile is a graph of NPV against discount rate. For a conventional project (outflow first, then inflows) it falls as the rate rises and crosses the horizontal axis at the IRR. For a single project NPV, IRR and B/C always give the same accept/reject decision, because NPV ≥ 0 at the MARR exactly when IRR ≥ MARR and B/C ≥ 1.

formulas.plainText: NPV = −P + sum over t = 1..n of CF_t / (1 + i)^t
B/C = PW of benefits / PW of costs

notes.text: For IRR interpolation choose two trial rates close together, one with positive and one with negative NPV; the wider the bracket, the larger the interpolation error.
Ranking mutually exclusive projects by their individual IRRs can give the wrong choice; use NPV or incremental IRR instead (see Comparison of Alternatives).
Payback is popular because it is easy and signals how quickly capital is recovered, but it is a screening tool: a project with a short payback can still have a negative NPV.

formulas.title: Net present value
formulas.plainText: NPV = sum over t = 0..n of CF_t / (1 + i)^t
formulas.description: Sum of all net cash flows discounted to time 0 at the MARR; accept if NPV is zero or positive.

formulas.title: IRR by linear interpolation
formulas.description: Estimates the rate at which NPV = 0 from a positive NPV1 at i1 and a negative NPV2 at i2.

formulas.title: Simple payback period
formulas.plainText: Payback = initial investment / uniform annual net inflow
formulas.description: Years to recover the investment from undiscounted equal annual inflows.

formulas.title: Benefit-cost ratio
formulas.plainText: B/C = PW of benefits / PW of costs
formulas.description: Public-project criterion; the project is justified when the ratio is 1 or more.

flashcards.back: The minimum attractive rate of return: the lowest rate of return a firm accepts on a new investment, based on cost of capital, opportunity cost and risk.

flashcards.front: How does discounted payback differ from simple payback?
flashcards.back: Discounted payback recovers the investment from cash flows discounted at the MARR, so it accounts for time value and is longer than simple payback.

flashcards.front: What is the IRR of a project?
flashcards.back: The discount rate at which the project's NPV is zero; accept the project if IRR is at least the MARR.

flashcards.front: What does the NPV profile show?
flashcards.back: NPV plotted against discount rate; for a conventional project it slopes downward and crosses zero at the IRR.

questions.questionText: A project costs Rs 10,000 and returns Rs 4,000 at the end of each year for 4 years. At a MARR of 10%, the discounted payback period is approximately:
questions.explanation: Cumulative PW at 10% after 3 years is 3,636 + 3,306 + 3,005 = 9,947, leaving 53 to recover from year 4's PW of 2,732: 3 + 53/2,732 ≈ 3.02 years. 2.5 years is the simple payback.

questions.questionText: An investment of Rs 1,00,000 yields Rs 40,000 at the end of each year for 3 years. At a MARR of 10% (P/A, 10%, 3 = 2.4869), the NPV and decision are:
questions.explanation: NPV = −1,00,000 + 40,000 × 2.4869 = −Rs 526. NPV is negative, so the project does not earn the MARR and is rejected, even though undiscounted inflows exceed the cost.

questions.questionText: A project's NPV is +Rs 500 at 10% and −Rs 300 at 15%. By linear interpolation its IRR is approximately:
An irrigation project has a present worth of benefits of Rs 15 crore and a present worth of costs of Rs 12 crore. Its B/C ratio and the decision are:
questions.explanation: B/C = 15/12 = 1.25. Since B/C ≥ 1, the benefits exceed the costs and the project is economically justified.

questions.questionText: For a single conventional project evaluated at the MARR, which statement is correct?
options: Payback and NPV always rank projects identically
NPV > 0, IRR > MARR and B/C > 1 always give the same accept decision
IRR is the rate at which the payback period equals the project life
questions.explanation: For a single conventional project NPV is positive exactly when the IRR exceeds the MARR and B/C exceeds 1, so the three criteria agree. Payback ignores time value and later flows, so it can disagree with NPV.

subtopics.title: Comparison of Alternatives
subtopics.subtitle: Mutually exclusive choices, unequal lives, incremental analysis and capitalised cost

concepts.text: Types of Alternatives

Engineering decisions usually involve choosing among alternatives that meet the same need, such as two pump models or two road alignments. Before comparing them, the analyst must know whether the alternatives are mutually exclusive or independent, whether they are revenue or cost (service) alternatives, and whether their lives are equal. Only the differences between alternatives matter; costs common to all can be ignored.

rows: Steel or concrete bridge at one site
Several unrelated projects within a budget
A valid alternative if not required

concepts.text: The do-nothing (null) alternative keeps the current situation and has zero incremental cash flow. It is chosen when no alternative earns the MARR. When a service must be provided (e.g. a legally required treatment plant), do-nothing is not available and the least-cost alternative is chosen.
Equal-Life Present Worth Comparison

When alternatives have equal lives, compute each one's present worth at the MARR over that life and select the one with the highest PW (for revenue alternatives) or lowest PW of costs (for cost alternatives). Costs can be entered as positive numbers when only costs are compared, as long as the convention is consistent.
Unequal Lives: LCM and Annual Worth
Two standard ways to compare alternatives with different lives:
items: Least common multiple (LCM) of lives: repeat each alternative's cash flows until all end together, then compare PW over that common study period (lives 4 and 6 years give 12 years).

Annual worth (AW): convert each alternative's cash flows to an equivalent uniform annual amount over its own life; because AW is the same for every repeated cycle, alternatives can be compared directly without the LCM.
Both methods assume repeatability: each alternative can be replaced by an identical one at the same costs.
When repeatability is unrealistic, a specified study period with estimated salvage values is used instead.

concepts.plainText: AW = −P(A/P, i, n) + S(A/F, i, n) − annual operating cost

concepts.text:
Unequal lives at MARR 10%, no salvage, equal O&M
Machine X: first cost Rs 10,000, life 3 yrs
  AW = 10,000 x (A/P,10%,3) = 10,000 x 0.40211 = Rs 4,021/yr
Machine Y: first cost Rs 15,000, life 6 yrs
  AW = 15,000 x (A/P,10%,6) = 15,000 x 0.22961 = Rs 3,444/yr
Select Y (lower equivalent annual cost)
LCM check: 6 years, X bought twice, same ranking
Incremental Analysis (IRR and B/C)

Choosing the alternative with the highest individual IRR or B/C can be wrong because a larger project may add more total value at a lower rate. Incremental analysis orders alternatives by first cost, then examines the extra (incremental) cash flow of the costlier one over the cheaper one. If the incremental IRR (ΔIRR) is at least the MARR, or the incremental B/C (ΔB/ΔC) is at least 1, the extra investment is justified and the costlier alternative becomes the defender; otherwise the cheaper one is kept.

MARR 10%, life 5 yrs (P/A,10%,5 = 3.7908)
          First cost  Annual benefit  NPV      IRR
A         10,000      3,000           +1,372   15.2%
B         15,000      4,200             +921   12.4%
B − A      5,000      1,200             −451    6.4%
ΔIRR 6.4% < MARR 10%: extra Rs 5,000 not justified -> choose A
Same answer as choosing the highest NPV
Capitalised Cost and Replacement Analysis

Capitalised cost is the present worth of a project assumed to last forever, such as a dam, canal or permanent road. Because P/A tends to 1/i as n becomes infinite, a perpetual annual cost A has present worth A/i. Replacement analysis compares an existing asset (defender) with a new one (challenger): the defender's first cost is its current market value, sunk costs such as its original price are ignored, and the comparison is usually made on equivalent annual worth.

concepts.plainText: Capitalised cost = initial cost + A / i

formulas.plainText: ΔNPV = NPV_B − NPV_A = PW of incremental cash flow (B − A)

notes.text: For unequal lives, annual worth is usually the quickest route in an MCQ: convert each first cost with A/P over its own life, add annual costs, subtract salvage × A/F, and compare.
Never compare present worths of alternatives with different lives directly over their own lives; this favours the shorter-lived option unfairly. Use the LCM or annual worth.
NPV, AW and incremental IRR or incremental B/C always pick the same alternative when applied correctly at the same MARR.

formulas.title: Annual worth
formulas.plainText: AW = −P(A/P, i, n) + S(A/F, i, n) − AOC
formulas.description: Equivalent uniform annual worth of an alternative over its own life, used to compare unequal lives.

formulas.title: Capitalised cost
formulas.description: Present worth of a perpetual project: initial cost plus perpetual annual cost divided by the interest rate.

formulas.title: Incremental B/C
formulas.description: Justifies the costlier alternative 2 over alternative 1 when the ratio is 1 or more.

flashcards.front: How do you compare two alternatives with lives of 4 and 6 years by present worth?
flashcards.back: Use a study period equal to the LCM of lives (12 years), repeating each alternative's cash flows, or compare annual worths instead.

flashcards.front: When is the costlier of two mutually exclusive alternatives chosen in incremental IRR analysis?
flashcards.back: When the IRR on the incremental investment (costlier minus cheaper) is at least the MARR.

flashcards.front: How is the original purchase price of an existing asset treated in replacement analysis?
flashcards.back: It is a sunk cost and ignored; the defender is valued at its current market value.

questions.questionText: Alternative P has a life of 4 years and alternative Q a life of 6 years. For a present-worth comparison using the repeatability assumption, the study period should be:
questions.explanation: The least common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12 years, so P is repeated three times and Q twice.

questions.questionText: A machine costs Rs 20,000, has a 5-year life and no salvage, and costs Rs 2,000 per year to operate. At 10% (A/P, 10%, 5 = 0.26380), its equivalent uniform annual cost is approximately:
A permanent canal costs Rs 10,00,000 to build and Rs 50,000 per year to maintain forever. At 5% interest its capitalised cost is:
Two mutually exclusive alternatives both have IRRs above the MARR. The IRR on the incremental investment of the costlier alternative over the cheaper one is below the MARR. The correct choice is:
questions.explanation: The extra investment does not earn the MARR, so it is not justified; the cheaper alternative, which itself earns more than the MARR, is selected.

questions.questionText: In a replacement study of an existing machine (defender) against a new one (challenger), the defender's first cost should be taken as:
questions.explanation: The original price is a sunk cost; the relevant opportunity cost of keeping the defender is what it could be sold for now, its market value.

subtopics.title: Depreciation & the Taxation System in Nepal
subtopics.subtitle: Depreciation methods, Nepal pool depreciation, tax types and after-tax cash flow

concepts.text: Purpose of Depreciation

Depreciation is the decrease in value of a physical asset with time and use, caused by wear and tear, deterioration, obsolescence or inadequacy. In accounting and taxation it is the systematic allocation of an asset's cost over its useful life. Depreciation is not a cash flow, but it is a tax-deductible expense, so it reduces taxable income and income tax and therefore affects after-tax cash flow.
Key terms used in depreciation calculations:
items: First cost (P): purchase price plus installation and commissioning costs.
Salvage value (S): estimated value at the end of useful life.
Useful life (n): period over which the asset is depreciated.
Book value (BV): first cost minus accumulated depreciation to date.
Market value: the price the asset would actually fetch, which may differ from book value.

concepts.text: Depreciation Methods

rows: d × BV at start of year

concepts.plainText: Straight line: D = (P − S)/n; BV_t = P − tD

concepts.text: In the sinking fund method, depreciation is treated as equal deposits A into a fund earning interest i, so that the fund equals P − S at the end of life. Depreciation in year t is the deposit plus the interest earned on the fund. For P = Rs 50,000, S = 0, n = 4 and i = 10%: A = 50,000 × 0.10/(1.1^4 − 1) = Rs 10,774 in year 1, and Rs 11,851 in year 2. Declining-balance methods never reach zero on their own; DDB is often switched to straight line in later years.
Depreciation under Nepal's Income Tax Act, 2058 (2002)

For tax purposes, Nepal's Income Tax Act, 2058 (2002) groups depreciable assets into pools (blocks) rather than depreciating each asset separately. Depreciation for each pool is computed by the declining-balance (written-down value) method on the pool's depreciation base, which is adjusted for additions and disposals during the year. The rates are prescribed in a schedule to the Act and, like other tax details, are subject to amendment by Finance Acts; the rates shown below are as per the Act's schedule and should be checked against the current law.

rows: Rate (as per Act, subject to amendment)
Buildings, structures and similar works of permanent nature
Computers, data-handling equipment, furniture, office equipment
Construction and earth-moving equipment and other assets not in other pools
Intangible assets (other than those in Pool D)

concepts.text: Taxation System in Nepal and After-Tax Cash Flow
Main taxes relevant to engineering projects in Nepal (rates set by the annual Finance Act, subject to amendment):
items: Income tax: direct tax on income of individuals and entities under the Income Tax Act, 2058 (2002); corporate rates vary by sector.
Value added tax (VAT): indirect tax on the value added at each stage of supply under the Value Added Tax Act, 2052 (1996); the standard rate is 13%, subject to amendment.
Customs duty: levied on imported (and some exported) goods under the Customs Act; significant for imported plant and equipment.
Excise duty: levied on specified goods produced or imported, such as alcohol, tobacco and vehicles.
Other levies include local taxes, registration fees and royalties (e.g. hydropower royalty).

concepts.plainText: After-tax cash flow = BTCF − tax rate × (BTCF − depreciation)

concepts.text: After-tax cash flow (ATCF) is the before-tax cash flow minus income tax, where tax is computed on taxable income = BTCF − depreciation. Example: BTCF Rs 1,00,000, depreciation Rs 20,000, tax rate 25%: taxable income 80,000, tax 20,000, ATCF 80,000. The tax saving from depreciation (t × D = Rs 5,000 here) is called the depreciation tax shield, and it is why faster depreciation improves a project's after-tax present worth.

formulas.latex: D_t = d \cdot BV_{t-1}, \qquad BV_t = P(1 - d)^{t}
formulas.plainText: Declining balance: D_t = d × BV_(t−1); BV_t = P(1 − d)^t

notes.text: For DDB questions the salvage value is not subtracted before applying the rate: D_t = (2/n) × book value at the start of year t, starting from the full first cost.

Tax rates, pool rates and thresholds in Nepal are revised through annual Finance Acts and amendments; quote them as 'as per the Act, subject to amendment' and rely on concepts (pooling, declining balance, tax types) in answers.
Depreciation itself is not a cash outflow; it matters in economic analysis only because it lowers taxable income and hence the tax paid.

formulas.title: Straight-line depreciation
formulas.description: Equal annual depreciation of first cost less salvage over the useful life.

formulas.title: Declining-balance book value
formulas.description: Book value after t years when a fixed rate d is applied to the opening book value each year (d = 2/n for DDB).

formulas.title: Sum-of-years-digits depreciation
formulas.description: Accelerated depreciation in year t using the remaining life divided by the sum of the years' digits.

formulas.title: After-tax cash flow
formulas.description: Cash flow after income tax, where tax is charged on before-tax cash flow less depreciation.

flashcards.back: First cost minus accumulated depreciation up to that time; it may differ from the asset's market value.

flashcards.front: How does Nepal's Income Tax Act, 2058 compute depreciation for tax?
flashcards.back: Assets are grouped into pools A to E, and each pool is depreciated by the declining-balance method on its depreciation base at rates set in the Act's schedule (subject to amendment).

flashcards.front: What is the depreciation tax shield?
flashcards.back: The tax saved because depreciation is deductible: tax rate × depreciation.

flashcards.front: Name four main taxes in Nepal's tax system.
flashcards.back: Income tax, value added tax (VAT), customs duty and excise duty.

questions.questionText: A machine costs Rs 1,00,000, has a salvage value of Rs 10,000 and a life of 5 years. Using straight-line depreciation, its book value at the end of year 2 is:
Equipment costing Rs 1,00,000 with a 5-year life is depreciated by the double-declining-balance method. The depreciation charge in year 2 is:
An asset costs Rs 60,000 with a salvage value of Rs 6,000 and a 5-year life. By the sum-of-years-digits method, the depreciation in year 3 is:
questions.explanation: SYD = 15; remaining life at start of year 3 is 3, so D3 = (60,000 − 6,000) × 3/15 = Rs 10,800.

questions.questionText: A project has a before-tax cash flow of Rs 1,00,000 in a year, depreciation of Rs 20,000 and an income tax rate of 25%. Its after-tax cash flow for that year is:
Under Nepal's Income Tax Act, 2058 (2002), tax depreciation of business assets is computed by:
options: Straight-line depreciation of each individual asset
Grouping assets into pools and applying declining-balance rates to each pool's depreciation base
The sinking fund method at the bank interest rate
Writing off the full cost in the year of purchase
questions.explanation: The Act uses a pooling (block) system: assets are classed into pools A to E and each pool is depreciated on a declining-balance basis at scheduled rates.
